text: Season two opens in Busan, at four in the morning, on a breakwater a kilometre long.
Jaeha staggers along in Auntie Geum's spare tracksuit, and she coaches him from a moped. Mostly about noodles.
Lyra, jogging backwards, sees no point in running from nothing. Nib answers like a soldier who has never had a day off.
At the lighthouse, he folds like a dropped coat.
Borro helpfully slings him over a shoulder like a sack of rice. Training over.
Not so fast. Geum's rule on carrying runs the other way.
Carrying is the Operator's job, so his body has to grow. Jaeha agrees, which is bad news for his legs.
Day one: capacity one hundred percent, body rated F. To Jaeha, numbers are made for going up.
He walks back on his own feet. Barely.
Five o'clock: item two on the timetable, the fish market's ice.
The aunties have opened a betting pool on how soon he drops one.
His forearms tremble, ice water dripping off his elbows.
Ice and mackerel explode across the floor, and the aunties settle up.
Borro strolls past with four crates on one shoulder, and the aunties fall in love. Mutual, give or take the smell.
Lyra recoils from a staring octopus. Nib quietly steals a fish cake.
Geum's answer to a dropped crate is another crate. Shaking, to her, is good news.
All that suffering, the window says, for less than half a percent.
Jaeha's eyes narrow. He reads windows like contracts.
And the small print says weight doesn't matter. Time does: about four percent an hour, held near his limit.
His arms shake, but his face goes cold. He has never been strong. He has always been patient.
So, polite as a student, he rewrites his own training: not heavy, but long.
Geum's gold tooth slowly appears. Right question.
Soon he's on an upturned tub, a tray of ice dead level on his forearms, writing notes. The aunties stop betting and stare.
One hour, four percent, as promised. Under the tray his fist closes, steadier.
Geum turns away and mutters half of yesterday's verdict. The S-rank half.
Six o'clock: tteokbokki, the one set nobody complains about. Borro joins in through the flap.
Nib stands at attention by the tent pole, until Geum hooks out a stool and relieves him of duty.
The Wall of Busan knows a wall-holder on sight. Nib's ears twitch.
Seoa calls while tying her school tie: her budget has booked him home for dinner. He promises seven o'clock, zero seconds to spare.
Then Bomi rings, pitching a Busan stream, and Geum vetoes it with her steel hand.
She hangs up, smug, and Jaeha weeps rivers into his cup.
Seven o'clock, one more set. Lyra wades into the surf instead and wrings out her silver braid in the sunrise like she owns the coast.
Two fishermen drop their net in the sea, and Jaeha walks his rice sack into a lamppost. Nib says nothing, loudly.
Across the harbour road, a black car waits in the shade, engine off.
Inside, Han Sora reports to Director Baek: the Operator is now a fishmonger's apprentice. Baek's orders stand. Hands off, eyes on.
On her other wrist, a new compass replaces the one Lyra shot off. Its needle leans toward the harbour.
That afternoon, dead fish line the shore.
Their scales shimmer violet along a thin dark crack.
It happened yesterday too, the fisherman says. Geum gives him nothing.
Her steel fingers twitch on their own, just like yesterday.
Yesterday's red window is back. Whatever is failing out there is still close.
He finally asks about that other carrier, from the night his parents died.
Geum doesn't turn. She answers the way she answers everything: with more training.
He protests to her back. For today, that night stays locked away.
Tuesday, four o'clock again. Still slow, but upright, knees actually lifting.
His cup of tteokbokki barely ripples now. Two days ago it slopped all over his knee.
Seven percent in two days, still an F. Progress at the speed of melting ice.
Busan's harshest judges compare notes. For once, Geum is the generous one.
That night Nib and Lyra spar in field form, and Jaeha carries both. Geum wants five minutes. He's at four forty, bleeding.
Under the lighthouse, Nib turns his ears to the sea. He once stood on a wall that fell. He knows this sound.
Nib is spent. In a gate, field form came back in a minute. Out here, it takes three hours.
Geum orders lights out. The four o'clock run waits for no one.
Near midnight, one old fisherman sits out on the tetrapods. Borro and Lyra are asleep against the parapet.
The water at his feet bubbles, and glows violet.
Something drags itself out: crab claws, an eel's tail, needle teeth, as long as a big dog.
The fisherman goes over backwards, screaming.
Jaeha sprints for the scream and calls Nib on instinct. But in rest form a summon can't fight, and the cooldown has hours left.
So Jaeha goes in himself, shoving the fisherman clear and taking the claw on his forearm.
On his back, bleeding, a second claw rising behind the first, he runs through his summons. There's no one to send.
Then pink rubber slippers slap down between him and the claws.
Auntie Geum, sixty-two and retired, raises her ladle at the monster while more claws break the glowing sea. The Wall of Busan is back on duty.
